When used about yourself ("I should have known better"), it is an honest and humble admission of a failure of judgment.

Here are several examples across different life situations so you can see how naturally this idiom fits in:

  • "You've been cooking for twenty years. You should know better than to leave the oil unattended on the stove." (Experience-based expectation)
  • "Honestly, I should have known better than to book a flight on New Year's Eve." (Personal regret)
  • "Don't scold the new intern too harshly — they don't know any better yet." (Excuse/sympathy)
  • "She's a lawyer. She knows better than to sign anything without reading the fine print." (Wisdom in action)
  • "I know better than to bring up politics at family dinners." (Learned from experience)

It is important to know what "know better" does not mean, so you don't confuse it.

It does not mean "to know more facts than someone." For example, if you say "I know better than my teacher about history," that is grammatically possible but it's a different use — it means "I know more than my teacher about history." This is a more literal, comparative meaning and not the idiom. The idiomatic use is always about wisdom, judgment, and avoiding foolish or wrong actions — not about knowing more facts on a topic.

Also, the idiom does not always mean someone is bad or evil. It simply means they failed to use the judgment they had available to them.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

If someone "knows better," they have the wisdom or experience to avoid doing something wrong or foolish.

If someone "should know better," they had that wisdom but failed to use it — and the speaker is mildly disappointed or critical.

If someone "should have known better," the mistake already happened and the speaker (or the person themselves) is reflecting that it was avoidable.

If someone "doesn't know any better," they are being excused — they genuinely lack the knowledge or experience to understand what they should do.

The idiom always lives in the space between wisdom and action — and it asks the pointed question: did you use the good sense you already have?
9518:
When you say you know something "just on an intellectual level," it means you understand it in your head — through thinking, reasoning, and logic — but you have not felt it emotionally or experienced it personally. Your brain has processed the information, but your heart and your gut have not truly absorbed it yet.

The word "just" is the most important word in this phrase. It signals a limitation. It tells the listener: "My understanding stops at thinking. It hasn't gone deeper than that."
Breaking It Down, Piece by Piece

"Know" — You have real knowledge. You are not ignorant. You have heard, read, or been taught the information.

"Just" — Only. Merely. Nothing more than. This word shrinks the knowledge down. It says: "My knowledge exists, but it is limited."

"On an intellectual level" — This means at the level of the mind, of logic and reasoning. The intellectual level is where facts, ideas, and concepts live. It is the level of thinking, not feeling or experiencing.

So together: "I understand this with my thinking mind, but only with my thinking mind — and nothing deeper."

This phrase almost always implies a contrast. There are different levels on which a person can "know" something:

  1. The intellectual level — You know it as a fact. Your brain accepts it as true.
  2. The emotional level — You feel it in your heart. It actually moves you.
  3. The visceral or gut level — You feel it in your body. It's raw and physical.
  4. The experiential level — You know it because you lived through it yourself.

When someone says they know something "just on an intellectual level," they are saying: "I have Level 1, but I am missing the deeper levels."

Think of it like reading about swimming versus actually jumping into water. You can read every book about swimming — what it feels like, how your body moves, how the water fills your lungs if you panic. You intellectually understand what swimming is. But the moment you jump in for the first time, you realize your intellectual knowledge only got you so far. The real experience is something else entirely.

Example 1 — Grief:
A young person who has never lost anyone close to them might say:

"I know, on an intellectual level, that losing a parent is devastating. But I've never gone through it, so I can't fully grasp how it must feel."

Here, the person has heard about grief, read about it, seen it in movies. Their brain understands that it is painful. But because they have never actually felt that loss, their understanding is only at the intellectual level.

Example 2 — Poverty:
Someone who grew up wealthy might say:

"I know on an intellectual level that many people can't afford food. I've seen the statistics. But I've never had to skip a meal because of money, so I don't truly feel what that's like."

The facts are in their head. But the hunger, the anxiety, the helplessness — those are not in their body or heart. So their knowledge stays at the intellectual level only.

Example 3 — Danger:
A soldier preparing for their first combat mission might say:

"I know intellectually that it will be dangerous. I've been trained and briefed. But I've never actually been in a firefight, so I can't fully know what fear in that moment actually feels like."

Training gives them knowledge. But experience gives something different that training cannot fully replicate.

Example 4 — Personal Growth:
Even in everyday life, a person might say:

"I know, intellectually, that I should stop worrying about what others think. I can explain all the reasons why it doesn't make sense to care. But when I'm actually standing in front of a crowd, my heart races anyway. I haven't internalized it."

This is a very common use — knowing the right thing with your mind, but your emotions haven't caught up yet.

People use this phrase to be honest about the limits of their understanding. It is a humble and precise thing to say. It signals:

  • "I am not claiming to fully understand this."
  • "My knowledge is real, but it is incomplete."
  • "Don't expect me to react the way someone with lived experience would."

It is also used to explain a gap — why someone might give advice that sounds smart but misses the emotional reality of a situation, or why someone might struggle to empathize even though they logically understand what another person is going through.
The Difference Between "Knowing" and "Knowing on an Intellectual Level"

This is the heart of it all. Consider these two sentences:

  • "I know that losing a child is the hardest thing a parent can go through."
  • "I know, on an intellectual level, that losing a child is the hardest thing a parent can go through."

The first sentence makes a straightforward claim. The second sentence is saying something more careful and more humble — "I know this as a fact, but I acknowledge that my knowledge is only at the surface. The true depth of this pain is beyond my current ability to understand."

The second version shows awareness of your own limitation.
Common Variations of the Same Idea

You will often hear similar phrases that carry exactly the same meaning:

  • "I know it in my head, but not in my heart."
  • "I understand it logically, but not emotionally."
  • "I get it rationally, but I haven't truly felt it."
  • "I know it theoretically."
  • "I know it abstractly."

All of these describe the same gap — the gap between thinking something and feeling or experiencing it.
One Sentence to Remember It Forever

If you ever forget the meaning, come back to this:

"Knowing something on an intellectual level means your brain has accepted a fact, but your heart and experience haven't lived it yet."

That gap — between the brain and the lived reality — is exactly what this phrase describes. It is a phrase about honesty, humility, and the recognition that true understanding often requires more than just thinking.
9519:
Know-how means practical knowledge — the kind of knowledge that actually allows you to do something, not just understand it in theory.

Think of it this way: you might read ten books about swimming. You'd know what strokes exist, how breathing works, what technique looks like. But that doesn't mean you can swim. The person who can actually get in the water, use the right technique, and move from one end of the pool to the other — that person has the know-how to swim. It is the "doing" kind of knowledge. It lives in experience, judgment, and practiced skill — not just in your head.

The best way to truly understand "know-how" is to see the difference between knowing about something and having know-how.

Knowing about something means you have information — facts, theories, concepts. You've read or studied the topic.

Know-how means you can actually execute it, handle it, and get results.

A medical student who has read thousands of pages about surgery knows about surgery. The experienced surgeon who can walk into an operating room, make the right decisions under pressure, and successfully complete the procedure — that surgeon has surgical know-how. The student has information; the surgeon has the practical, battle-tested ability to perform.

This gap between knowing about and knowing how is exactly what the word captures.

Know-how is almost always built through experience, training, and practice over time. It's the kind of ability that is very hard to transfer purely through words or books. You develop it by actually doing the thing — making mistakes, learning from them, refining your approach, and eventually reaching a point where you can handle the task with confidence and competence.

This is why know-how is considered valuable. Anyone can read a book. Not everyone can develop the real, working ability that the book describes.
The range of what it describes

Know-how can apply to virtually any field or area of life, from highly technical domains to everyday tasks.

In technical and professional fields: "The engineer's know-how in structural design made the project a success." Or: "The startup lacked the financial know-how to manage its cash flow."

In business and leadership: "She was hired specifically for her marketing know-how." Or: "Running a restaurant requires both culinary and management know-how."

In everyday life: "I don't have the know-how to fix a leaking pipe." Or: "He has the know-how to grow vegetables even in poor soil."

In all of these, the pattern is the same — it's not just awareness of the subject, it's the real, practiced ability to handle it effectively.
What the word implies about a person

When you say someone has the know-how, you are making a quiet but meaningful compliment. You are saying they are not just a person who has read about the topic — they are someone who can be trusted to actually get it done. It carries a sense of competence, reliability, and experience.

Saying "She has the know-how to manage a crisis" means she knows what steps to take, can make sound decisions under pressure, and has the experience to back it up. It's a confident endorsement of someone's practical ability.

Conversely, saying "I lack the know-how" is an honest admission that while you may understand the topic at a surface level, you don't yet have the hands-on ability to handle it.

Know-how is an uncountable noun, which is important to get right.

You cannot say "a know-how" or "know-hows" — these are grammatically wrong. You always treat it as a mass concept, the same way you treat words like "information" or "advice."

The most common patterns are:

"Have the know-how to [do something]" — "Does she have the know-how to lead this project?"

"Lack the know-how" — "Many beginners lack the technical know-how to set up a server."

"[Adjective] know-how" — Know-how is very frequently combined with an adjective that tells you what area the know-how belongs to: technical know-how, financial know-how, business know-how, practical know-how, marketing know-how, engineering know-how. This is one of the most natural and common ways the word appears.

"Someone's know-how" — "The company is built on its founder's know-how in logistics."
How it compares to similar words

Know-how vs. Knowledge. Knowledge is a broader word that includes facts, theories, history, and information of all kinds — even purely academic knowledge that you can never apply. Know-how is always specifically about the ability to do something. A philosopher may have deep knowledge of ethics but no know-how in carpentry.

Know-how vs. Skill. These are the closest in meaning and are often interchangeable. However, "skill" tends to refer to one specific, well-defined ability — "she has good writing skills." Know-how is slightly broader and more holistic — it suggests a combination of skill, experience, and practical judgment all working together. When someone has know-how in an area, they can handle not just the easy, predictable parts of a task but also the unexpected challenges that arise.

Know-how vs. Expertise. Expertise implies a very high, professional-grade level of mastery, often in a specialized field. Know-how is more flexible — it can describe someone's ability at any level, from basic to advanced. A teenager who knows how to change a tire has the know-how to do it. A Formula 1 pit crew member has expertise in tire changes.
The tone and register of the word

Know-how sits comfortably between informal and professional language. It is not slang, but it's also not stiff or overly academic. You'll hear it in casual conversation ("Do you have the know-how to fix this?"), in business discussions ("We need someone with the right know-how"), and in professional writing. It's a widely respected, universally understood word in English.
A final image to lock it in

Imagine a detailed recipe book for a complex French dish. Anyone can buy the book and read every page. That gives them knowledge about the dish — the ingredients, the steps, the theory. But the chef who has made that dish hundreds of times, who knows instinctively when the sauce needs more time, how to rescue it if something goes wrong, and exactly how it should taste at each stage — that chef has know-how. The book can be copied and given to a million people. The know-how cannot be passed on just by handing over the book. It has to be lived, practiced, and earned. That earned, practical, results-producing ability is exactly what the word means.
9520: A know-it-all is a person who behaves as if they know everything about every topic — and, importantly, makes sure that everyone around them is aware of it. It is a word used to describe not just what a person knows, but how they act about it. The emphasis is on the attitude, not the knowledge itself.

A know-it-all typically shows several recognizable behaviors:

  • They almost never say "I don't know." Even when they are unsure, they will confidently give an answer as if they are certain.
  • They love to correct others, often jumping in to point out mistakes — even when nobody asked.
  • They dismiss other people's opinions or ideas quickly, as if those opinions are not even worth considering.
  • They talk over people or interrupt them, because in their mind, they already know what the other person is about to say — and they think they know better anyway.
  • They rarely, if ever, admit they were wrong, even when proven so.
  • They often give unsolicited advice — meaning they offer their knowledge or opinions even when no one has asked for it.

Think of that one person in a classroom who raises their hand for every single question, sighs loudly when someone else gives a wrong answer, and always has to add something extra even after the teacher has already explained everything. That is a classic know-it-all.
The Tone of the Word — Is It Positive or Negative?

This is an insult, or at least a criticism. It is never a compliment.

When you call someone a know-it-all, you are not praising their intelligence. You are criticizing their arrogance and their annoying behavior. The problem with a know-it-all is not that they are smart — it is that they act superior, as if no one else's knowledge or experience is valuable.

Interestingly, a know-it-all is not necessarily even correct all the time. They simply behave as though they are. Real expertise is usually paired with humility — a truly knowledgeable person tends to understand how much they don't know. A know-it-all, by contrast, has the opposite attitude: they are overconfident, closed-minded, and condescending.
A Crucial Distinction: Being Knowledgeable vs. Being a Know-It-All

This is one of the most important things to understand about this word. These two things are not the same:

  • A knowledgeable person knows a lot, shares it when appropriate, listens to others, and accepts being wrong gracefully.
  • A know-it-all may or may not actually know a lot, but acts as though they know everything, does not genuinely listen, and finds it very difficult to accept correction.

So the word is really about attitude and behavior, not about intelligence or knowledge level. You could be the smartest person in the room and still not be a know-it-all. And you could be quite ordinary in your knowledge and still be one.
The Register — When and Where Is This Word Used?

"Know-it-all" is an informal, everyday word. You would use it in casual conversation — with friends, family, or colleagues — but you would not use it in a formal essay, a business report, or an academic paper. In formal writing, you might instead use words like arrogant, presumptuous, or overconfident.

Here are several examples showing how this word is used naturally:

  • "Don't bother explaining it to Derek — he's such a know-it-all that he'll just interrupt you halfway through."
  • "She's brilliant, but she can come across as a know-it-all at meetings because she never lets anyone else finish a thought."
  • "I used to be a bit of a know-it-all in school. I've learned to listen more since then."
  • "Nobody likes working with a know-it-all — it makes everyone else feel small."

Notice that in all these examples, the word carries a negative judgment. Even in the third example, where the speaker is talking about themselves, they are looking back with some embarrassment or self-criticism.

Several other words carry a similar meaning, each with a slight difference in flavor:

  • Smarty-pants — similar meaning, but slightly more playful and less harsh. Often used with children or in a lighthearted way.
  • Wiseacre — an older, slightly old-fashioned word for a know-it-all; someone who makes clever remarks and acts superior.
  • Smart aleck (also smart alec) — someone who is cocky and likes to make sarcastic or clever remarks to show they are smarter than others.
  • Pedant — a more formal word for someone who obsessively corrects small details or insists on displaying their knowledge of rules, often in an irritating way.
  • Blowhard — someone who boasts and talks a lot about themselves and what they know, in an exaggerated way.

Among these, "know-it-all" is the most common, the most direct, and the most broadly understood in everyday English.

The opposite of a know-it-all is someone who is open-minded, humble, and a good listener — someone who acknowledges the limits of their knowledge and genuinely values what other people have to say. In a single word, the opposite quality might be called humility.

A know-it-all (noun) is a person who acts as though they have all the answers on all topics, constantly shows off this supposed knowledge, dismisses or talks over others, and rarely admits being wrong — all in an arrogant and often irritating way. The word is informal, always negative in tone, and focuses on a person's attitude rather than their actual level of knowledge.
9521:
"Knowingly" means: in a way that shows full awareness — while being completely aware of what you are doing, what is true, or what the situation is.

The central question "knowingly" answers is: Did the person know what was happening when it happened?

If yes — they did it knowingly.

Sense 1 — With full awareness (the primary, most common sense)

When someone does something "knowingly," they did it with complete, clear awareness — not by accident, not out of confusion, not because they were tricked.

  • She knowingly broke the rules. → She knew she was breaking the rules when she did it.
  • He knowingly gave false information. → He was fully aware that what he said was false.
  • The company knowingly sold defective products. → The company knew the products were defective and sold them anyway.

Notice what "knowingly" adds to each sentence: it tells you that awareness was present. The action didn't happen in ignorance. The person knew.

Sense 2 — In a way that expresses private or shared understanding (the expressive, literary sense)

This sense is about body language and expression. When someone smiles, looks, or nods "knowingly," their face or gesture communicates a quiet, unspoken understanding — often something others in the room don't know, or something private between two people.

  • She smiled knowingly. → Her smile said: "I know what's really going on here."
  • He looked at me knowingly. → His look communicated a silent, shared understanding between us — without words.
  • They exchanged knowing glances. (adjective form) → They shared a look that silently said: "We both know."

This sense appears often in novels and storytelling to describe a character who secretly understands something. The expression — the smile, the look, the nod — is the outward signal of inner awareness.
The Heart of the Word: Awareness vs. Intention

This is an important nuance that many learners miss.

"Knowingly" is primarily about awareness — it tells you the person knew. It is not exactly the same as "deliberately" or "intentionally," which tell you the person wanted a particular outcome. However, in practice, these meanings overlap heavily.

Here's how they differ:

  • Knowingly → "I was aware of what I was doing / what was true."
  • Deliberately / Intentionally → "I chose to do this on purpose; I wanted this outcome."

In the sentence "He knowingly took a risk" — it means he was aware there was a risk when he acted. It doesn't necessarily mean he wanted something bad to happen; it means he wasn't in the dark about the risk.

In the sentence "He deliberately took a risk" — it emphasizes the choice, the act of will.

In most real-world uses, the two overlap — because if you do something while being fully aware, you're usually also choosing to do it. But the defining quality of "knowingly" is always awareness. That's its heart.

This is where "knowingly" carries its most precise and important weight. In law, "knowingly" is a specific mental state that determines whether a person can be held responsible for an action.

If you did something knowingly, you cannot claim it was an accident or that you had no idea what was happening. The law uses "knowingly" to establish that the person was fully conscious of their action and of the relevant facts at the time.

  • She was found guilty of knowingly concealing evidence. → She knew the evidence existed and knew she was hiding it.
  • The manufacturer knowingly ignored safety defects. → The manufacturer was aware of the defects and chose to proceed anyway.

In legal thinking, "knowingly" is a higher standard than "recklessly" or "negligently":

  • Knowingly → You actually knew what you were doing or what the facts were.
  • Recklessly → You were aware of a risk but ignored it carelessly.
  • Negligently → You should have known, but failed to find out.

A person who acts "knowingly" is generally seen as more culpable (more at fault) than one who acted recklessly or negligently — because "knowingly" implies the clearest form of conscious awareness.

These two are exact opposites, and the contrast between them is powerful.

  • Knowingly → with full awareness
  • Unknowingly → without any awareness; without realizing

Side-by-side examples:

  • She knowingly signed a fraudulent document. → She knew it was fraudulent.
  • She unknowingly signed a fraudulent document. → She had no idea it was fraudulent; she was deceived.

The difference here is not just semantic — it is moral and legal. When you do something knowingly, you bear far greater responsibility. When you do something unknowingly, you were in the dark, and your culpability is reduced or eliminated.

These two words sound similar but mean very different things.

  • Knowingly → with awareness of something specific, at a specific moment in time
  • Knowledgeably → with expertise; in a way that shows broad, deep knowledge of a subject

Examples:

  • She spoke knowledgeably about climate science. → She demonstrated deep, expert understanding of the topic.
  • She knowingly ignored the warnings about climate science. → She was fully aware the warnings existed when she ignored them.

"Knowledgeably" is about how much you know on a subject in general. "Knowingly" is about whether you were aware of something at a particular moment. One is about expertise; the other is about conscious awareness.

"Knowingly" often carries a moral charge in a sentence — especially when paired with something negative. This is because awareness implies choice. If you knew something was wrong and still did it, your moral responsibility is far greater than if you had no idea.

  • He knowingly misled her. → He knew he was misleading her. (This feels worse than simply "he misled her.")
  • They knowingly put people at risk. → They were aware of the danger and acted anyway. (This feels like a serious accusation.)

The word "knowingly" draws attention to the moment of awareness — it says: there was a moment when this person knew, and they acted anyway.

However, "knowingly" doesn't always have a negative charge. It simply describes awareness:

  • She knowingly accepted a difficult challenge. → She went in with her eyes open, fully aware of how hard it would be.

Here it carries no moral condemnation — just clarity about awareness.

1. Legal and official documents — This is where "knowingly" is most precise and technical. Courts, laws, contracts, and regulations use it frequently. (Whoever knowingly makes a false statement shall be punished...)
  2. News and journalism — To describe deliberate, aware action, especially wrongdoing. (The firm knowingly misled investors for years.)
  3. Literature and storytelling — Especially in Sense 2, to describe a look or expression that signals unspoken understanding. (She smiled at him knowingly, as if she had known all along.)
  4. Everyday speech — Less common than in formal writing, but not unusual. People more often say "she knew exactly what she was doing" or "he did it on purpose" in conversation — but "knowingly" fits in naturally when you want precision.

Core meaningWith full awareness; while being fully aware
Sense 1Doing something while knowing what you're doing or what is true (main sense)
Sense 2Expressing, through a look or gesture, a quiet, unspoken understanding (expressive sense)
Key qualityAwareness — the person knew
OppositeUnknowingly (without awareness)
Don't confuse withKnowledgeably (with expertise on a subject)
Legal meaningA specific mental state: the person was fully aware of their action and the facts
Moral weightCarries heavier responsibility than accidental or uninformed action

The deepest truth about "knowingly" is this: it is a word about the presence of consciousness at the moment of action. It says — this person was not in the dark. They knew. And with that knowledge, they acted. Whether that action was wrong, brave, hidden, or deliberate depends on the sentence — but "knowingly" always tells you that the light was on inside their mind.
9522: Knowledge is the state of genuinely holding something true in your mind, with good reason to believe it. When you say you know something, you're claiming more than guessing or feeling — you're saying that what you hold in your mind correctly reflects reality, and that you have a solid basis for holding it.
The Classic Definition: Justified True Belief

For centuries, the most widely accepted definition of knowledge is justified true belief. This means three things must all be true at once:

1. It must be true. You cannot know something false. If someone in ancient times "knew" that the Sun revolves around the Earth, they did not actually have knowledge — they had a false belief. Truth is non-negotiable for knowledge.

2. You must believe it. A fact sitting in an unread book isn't anyone's knowledge. You have to genuinely hold something as true in your mind for it to be your knowledge.

3. You must have justification. If you guess that it will rain tomorrow and it does rain, you were right — but you didn't know it would rain. Justification means you have good reason, evidence, or a reliable basis for your belief. A lucky guess doesn't count.

Put simply: Knowledge = a true belief that you have good reason to hold.
A Famous Challenge: The Gettier Problem

In 1963, philosopher Edmund Gettier showed that meeting all three conditions might still not be enough to guarantee knowledge. His examples involve situations where someone has a justified true belief, but only by coincidence — and we'd hesitate to call that knowledge.

A simple version: imagine you glance at a clock on the wall. It reads 3:00. Your belief is true — it really is 3:00. And you're justified in trusting the clock. But unknown to you, the clock stopped exactly 12 hours ago. You happened to look at it at the right moment. You got lucky. Did you know it was 3:00?

Most people feel the answer is no — and this is the Gettier problem. It shows that knowledge is slightly more elusive than the three-part definition suggests. Philosophers have proposed many fixes, but there's still no universal agreement on the perfect definition. For everyday and practical purposes, justified true belief remains the most useful and widely used starting point.

Knowledge isn't one single thing — it comes in meaningfully different forms.

1. Knowing that — Propositional Knowledge

This is knowledge of facts. It takes the form "I know that...":

  • "I know that water is made of hydrogen and oxygen."
  • "I know that India became independent in 1947."

These are statements that are either true or false, and when you know them, you hold the true ones correctly. This is the type of knowledge most discussed in education and intellectual life.

2. Knowing how — Procedural Knowledge

This is knowledge of how to do something. "I know how to swim." "I know how to ride a bicycle." You might be able to do something skillfully without being able to explain it in words. A skilled musician might not be able to describe how their fingers find the right notes — but they know how. This kind of knowledge lives in practice, habit, and the body, not just in language and facts.

3. Knowing of — Acquaintance Knowledge

This is knowing something through direct experience or personal familiarity. "I know Paris" — meaning you've been there, you've walked its streets. "I know her" — meaning you've met and interacted with her. You can know hundreds of facts about Paris without ever having visited — but in this sense, you don't "know Paris." Acquaintance knowledge comes from direct, first-hand contact.
How Knowledge Differs from Closely Related Words

This is where understanding the word "knowledge" gets sharper.

Knowledge vs. Information
Information is raw data or facts that exist in the world — in books, databases, or on the internet. Knowledge is what happens when that information is genuinely grasped by a mind. A library holds vast information, but the library itself knows nothing. Knowledge requires a knower.

Knowledge vs. Belief
A belief is anything you accept as true in your mind — but beliefs can be false. You might firmly believe something incorrect. Knowledge requires the belief to actually be true and to be justified. All knowledge involves belief, but not all belief is knowledge. Knowledge is a specific, qualified kind of belief.

Knowledge vs. Opinion
An opinion is a view you hold, especially on matters involving judgment, values, or interpretation. Opinions can be thoughtful or shallow, well-supported or poorly supported. But even a carefully held opinion on a genuinely contested question isn't usually called "knowledge" — knowledge implies a higher degree of certainty and a firmer factual basis.

Knowledge vs. Understanding
Understanding goes deeper than knowledge. To know something is to hold a fact correctly. To understand it is to grasp why it's true, how it connects to other things, and to see the bigger picture. You might know that mixing an acid and a base produces a neutralization reaction — but understanding chemistry means grasping the mechanism, the patterns, the implications. Knowledge is a building block; understanding is what you build with it. You can have knowledge without understanding, but you cannot have deep understanding without knowledge.

Knowledge vs. Wisdom
Wisdom is the ability to use knowledge and understanding well — to make sound judgments, act appropriately, and know what truly matters in a given situation. Wisdom is the mature, lived application of knowledge over time and experience. A person can accumulate enormous knowledge and still act foolishly. And wisdom often includes knowing the limits of one's own knowledge — knowing what you don't know. You can have knowledge without wisdom, but wisdom almost always contains knowledge.

Knowledge reaches us through several distinct pathways:

Experience and perception. We see, hear, touch, smell, and interact with the world around us, and we learn from it directly. This is the most fundamental and immediate source of knowledge.

Reasoning. By thinking carefully and drawing logical conclusions from what we already know, we can arrive at new knowledge — including about things we have never directly observed. Mathematics and logic are prime examples.

Testimony. Much of what we know, we were told — by teachers, books, trusted people, or reliable institutions. We take on their knowledge by trusting their credibility. Most of your knowledge about history, science, and the world at large came through testimony.

Memory. Knowledge gained in the past must be stored and recalled to remain useful. Without memory, every moment would begin from zero.

Introspection. We can know things about our own inner life — our thoughts, feelings, sensations, and desires — in a way no one else can access directly. You know you're in pain; you know you're feeling happy. This is knowledge of yourself from the inside.

Knowledge has real boundaries, and recognizing them is a mark of intellectual honesty.

There are things that are currently unknown — humanity hasn't figured them out yet. There are things that may be unknowable in principle — questions where no amount of evidence or reasoning can fully settle the matter. There are also things we think we know but are actually wrong about — confident false belief that masquerades as knowledge.

Acknowledging what you don't know is not a weakness; it is the very foundation of honest thinking, good science, and continued learning. The philosopher Socrates famously said that true wisdom begins with knowing the limits of one's own knowledge.

Knowledge can belong to a single person, or it can be held collectively. A doctor has medical knowledge. A culture carries knowledge passed down through generations — stories, practices, observations about the world. Libraries, universities, and scientific institutions exist to preserve, verify, and transmit the collective knowledge of humanity across time.

When someone says "we know" — as in "we know the Earth is about 4.5 billion years old" — they mean that this is part of humanity's collective body of verified knowledge, even if any single person hasn't personally checked every piece of evidence.

Knowledge is a true belief that you are justified in holding. It is more than a guess, more than an opinion, and more than mere information — it requires truth, belief, and justification together. It comes in factual, practical, and experiential forms. It is deeper than information, less complete than understanding, and the foundation of wisdom. It enters the mind through experience, reasoning, testimony, memory, and introspection. And it has genuine limits — which honest thinkers embrace rather than ignore.
9523:
"Knuckle under" means to give in, submit, or surrender — especially when someone forces you to, or when pressure becomes too great to resist.

When a person "knuckles under," they stop resisting and accept defeat, even if they don't want to. The key feeling here is reluctance — the person giving in does not do so happily. They are pushed into submission.

Think of it simply: you are fighting back or holding your ground, but eventually the pressure — from a person, a situation, or circumstances — becomes too much, and you cave in.
A Simple, Vivid Example

Imagine a student who hates a school rule about uniforms. For weeks, he refuses to wear it and argues with the principal. But after the principal threatens him with suspension, he finally wears the uniform.

➡️ He knuckled under to the principal's authority.

He didn't want to comply. He was made to. That's the heart of the phrase.
Breaking Down the Word "Knuckle"

You might wonder — what do knuckles (the bumpy joints on your fingers) have to do with giving in?

The answer lies in history and old body language.

In older English, the word "knuckle" referred not only to finger joints but also more broadly to knee and leg joints in both humans and animals. Even today, you'll hear "a knuckle of veal" — which refers to the knee/shin area of a calf.

Now think about what humans do when they surrender or bow to someone more powerful — they bend their knees and kneel down. Kneeling is one of the oldest, most universal gestures of submission in the world. Soldiers knelt before kings. Servants knelt before masters.

So "knuckling under" originally evoked the image of bending your joints downward — of literally lowering your body before another person as a sign that you accept their power over you.

Over time, this physical image became a metaphor for any kind of psychological or social surrender.
The Feeling Inside the Phrase

This is important: "knuckle under" almost always carries a negative emotional charge. It is not neutral.

When you say someone "knuckled under," you are subtly suggesting one or more of these things:

  • They gave up when they perhaps shouldn't have.
  • They were forced into it — not willing.
  • There is something slightly shameful or weak about the act of giving in.
  • The person or force they gave in to was dominant, controlling, or unfair.

This is very different from, say, agreeing with someone, or compromising with someone. Those words feel balanced and respectful. "Knuckle under" feels like defeat under pressure.
How It Is Used in Sentences

Here are several examples showing the phrase in different situations. Notice how in every case, someone is being pushed and eventually gives in:

  • "She refused to knuckle under to her boss's unreasonable demands, even at the risk of losing her job." (She resisted pressure from authority.)
  • "After months of protests, the government finally knuckled under and agreed to reform the law." (An institution gave in to public pressure.)
  • "Don't knuckle under just because people disagree with you — stand your ground if you believe you're right." (Advice not to give in too easily.)
  • "He knuckled under to peer pressure and did something he later deeply regretted." (Social pressure forced a bad decision.)
  • "The small business was forced to knuckle under to the demands of its giant corporate partner." (Weaker party surrenders to a stronger one.)
What Can You "Knuckle Under" To?

The phrase works with many kinds of pressures. You can knuckle under to:

  • A person — a boss, a bully, a parent, a ruler.
  • An institution or authority — a government, a company, a court.
  • Social pressure — what other people expect or demand of you.
  • Circumstances — difficult situations that leave you no choice.
  • Threats or intimidation — when someone uses fear to force you to comply.
What "Knuckle Under" Is NOT

It helps to know what this phrase does not mean, so you don't confuse it with similar-sounding ideas:

ConceptHow It's Different
  • "Knuckle down" — This is a completely different phrase. It means to start working hard and seriously on something. ("I need to knuckle down and finish this report.") One phrase means to give in; the other means to buckle up and focus.
  • "Give up" — This is similar but broader. You can "give up" on a hobby, a goal, or a relationship. "Knuckle under" is more specific — it's about submitting to someone or something that has power over you.
  • "Compromise" — Compromise means both sides give something up. "Knuckle under" means only one side surrenders, usually the weaker one.
  • "Agree" — If you agree with someone, you genuinely share their view. If you "knuckle under," you go along with them even though you disagree, because you have no other choice.
The Tone: When Do People Use This Phrase?

"Knuckle under" is used in everyday spoken and written English. It appears in:

  • Conversations about politics and power ("Will the opposition party knuckle under to the coalition's demands?")
  • Workplace scenarios ("She refused to knuckle under to her manager's bullying.")
  • Personal relationships ("He always knuckles under whenever his partner gets angry.")
  • Historical writing ("The colony was forced to knuckle under to imperial rule.")

It is informal to semi-formal in tone — perfectly natural in conversation, news writing, and essays, but you would likely use more formal phrasing like "capitulate" or "yield" in very official or academic writing.
Synonyms — Words That Mean the Same Thing

If you want to express the same idea with different words, you can use:

  • Yield to (slightly more formal)
  • Submit to (more formal, stronger)
  • Cave in (very casual, same emotional feeling as "knuckle under")
  • Capitulate (formal; often used in politics and military contexts)
  • Back down (suggests retreating from a position you held)
  • Give in (the most neutral and common everyday alternative)
  • Bow to (carries a strong sense of acknowledging someone's power)
  • Succumb to (suggests being worn down or overwhelmed)
The Opposite

If "knuckle under" means to give in, the opposite ideas include:

  • Stand firm / stand your ground — refusing to give in despite pressure.
  • Hold out — resisting for a long time without surrendering.
  • Defy — actively going against authority or pressure.
  • Resist — pushing back against force or demands.
One-Line Summary to Remember Forever

"Knuckle under" means to reluctantly submit or surrender to pressure, force, or authority — to give in when someone or something pushes you hard enough, even when you don't want to.

If you remember just one image: picture someone being pushed to their knees — not because they want to kneel, but because the force against them is too strong. That is the spirit of "knuckle under."
9524:
To knuckle down means to start working seriously, with full focus and strong effort, especially on a task that is difficult or demanding. When someone knuckles down, they stop wasting time, stop being distracted, and commit themselves fully to getting something done.

Think of it this way: imagine a student who has been watching TV all evening while their homework sits untouched. Then, at 9 PM, they turn off the TV, sit at their desk, and get fully absorbed in their work. That moment of switching to serious, determined effort — that is knuckling down.

It is not just about working. It is about working with intention, discipline, and real commitment.
Where Did This Phrase Come From?

The origin of "knuckle down" comes from a very old children's game — marbles.

In the traditional game of marbles, there was a rule that when you took your shot, you had to place your knuckle flat on the ground before flicking the marble with your thumb. This position was called "knuckling down." It required you to get low, steady yourself, focus carefully, and give the shot your full attention and precision.

Over time, this physical act of getting down low and focusing hard became a metaphor for applying serious effort to anything in life — not just marbles. The phrase has been used in the English language since at least the mid-1700s, making it quite an old expression.
How It Is Used in Grammar

"Knuckle down" is a phrasal verb — that means it is a verb ("knuckle") combined with a small word ("down") that together create a new meaning.

It is most commonly used in two patterns:

Pattern 1: Knuckle down (on its own)
This means to simply start working hard, without specifying the task.

"The deadline is tomorrow. It's time to knuckle down."

Pattern 2: Knuckle down to + something
Here, you name the specific task you are going to work hard on.

"She finally knuckled down to her revision."
"He needs to knuckle down to the project."

Both patterns are correct. The second one is just more specific.

Here are examples showing the phrase in different everyday situations, so you can see how naturally it fits:

At school:
"You've been distracted all week. If you want to pass your exams, you need to knuckle down and study."

At work:
"The team had a slow start, but once the pressure came, they really knuckled down and finished the report on time."

In sports:
"After losing the first half, the players knuckled down in the second half and turned the match around."

Personal habits:
"I kept putting off learning Spanish for months. I finally knuckled down last January, and now I can hold a basic conversation."

As advice:
"Stop overthinking it and just knuckle down — the only way through is to do the work."

An important nuance — a subtle but important detail — is that "knuckle down" almost always carries the idea of a shift or a change. It implies that before this moment, the person was not working as hard as they should have been. Maybe they were procrastinating, being lazy, getting distracted, or avoiding the task.

When someone knuckles down, there is a turning point — a moment of decision where they say, in effect, "Enough. I am going to get serious now."

This makes the phrase slightly more powerful than just saying "work hard." It carries a sense of determination rising up from within a person — a conscious decision to stop drifting and start doing.

"Knuckle down" is an informal expression. It is perfectly natural in everyday conversation, in casual writing, in sports commentary, in schools, and in workplaces. However, you would not typically use it in a very formal academic essay or an official legal document. In those contexts, you would say something like "apply oneself diligently" instead.

It is used in both British English and American English, so you will encounter it widely across the English-speaking world.
Do Not Confuse It With "Knuckle Under"

This is a very important distinction, because learners sometimes mix these up.

"Knuckle down" = to work hard and apply serious effort. (Positive, determined action.)

"Knuckle under" = to give in to pressure or authority; to surrender or submit to someone else's will against your own wishes. (Often negative or reluctant.)

Example of "knuckle under":
"The workers were forced to knuckle under when the company threatened job cuts."

Here, nobody is working harder — they are simply giving in. The two phrases have completely opposite emotional directions. "Knuckle down" is about rising to a challenge; "knuckle under" is about collapsing under pressure.
Similar Phrases with the Same Meaning

English has several other expressions that carry a similar meaning to "knuckle down." Knowing them will help you understand conversations more easily:

"Buckle down" — extremely similar in meaning; perhaps the closest alternative. "You need to buckle down and finish this."

"Get down to business" — to stop small talk or delays and focus on what needs to be done.

"Put your nose to the grindstone" — to work hard and continuously without stopping.

"Roll up your sleeves" — to prepare for hard work; to get ready to tackle something seriously.

"Bear down" — to try harder and focus more intensely, especially under pressure.

All of these share the idea of increased seriousness and effort, but "knuckle down" remains one of the most vivid and commonly used.

"Knuckle down" means to stop delaying, focus completely, and work hard on something that matters. It comes from the old marble-playing tradition of pressing your knuckle to the ground to take a careful, precise shot. Today, it describes any moment when a person makes a determined decision to apply real, serious effort — especially after a period of laziness, distraction, or procrastination. It is informal, widely used in both British and American English, and should never be confused with "knuckle under," which means the opposite.
9525:
Knurled describes a surface that has been intentionally covered with a pattern of tiny, repeated ridges or bumps. The purpose is almost always the same: to give your fingers something to grip onto so the object doesn't slip.

Think of it this way — if you've ever held a metal pen where the lower section feels slightly rough and patterned under your fingers (rather than smooth), that textured section is knurled.
What Does the Pattern Actually Look Like?

The ridges on a knurled surface aren't random. They follow a deliberate, orderly pattern. There are two common types:

Straight knurling — the ridges run in parallel lines along the length of the object, like tiny train tracks wrapping around it.

Diamond knurling — two sets of lines cross each other diagonally, creating a repeated diamond or crosshatch pattern across the surface. This is the most common type you'll encounter. Think of it like a miniature waffle pattern pressed into metal.

The ridges themselves are small — often just a fraction of a millimetre deep — but they are very noticeable to the touch.
Why Do Objects Have Knurled Surfaces?

The entire reason knurling exists is grip and control. When your fingers press against a knurled surface, those tiny ridges create friction between your skin and the object. This prevents the object from rotating or sliding out of your grasp, even if your hands are slightly wet or oily.

This matters a lot in precise or mechanical contexts — for example, when you need to turn a small screw by hand, or adjust a fine dial with your fingertips. A smooth surface would spin uselessly; a knurled one stays under your control.

Knurling appears almost exclusively on manufactured metal (or hard plastic) objects — particularly ones that need to be gripped, twisted, or turned by hand. Common examples:

  • The barrel of a high-quality pen or mechanical pencil, where your thumb and fingers rest
  • The focus or zoom ring on a camera lens
  • Small adjustment screws (called thumbscrews) on technical equipment
  • Volume or tuning knobs on older audio equipment
  • The handle section of precision instruments like scalpels or dental tools
  • Certain bolts and nuts designed to be tightened by hand without a wrench
  • Gun components, like trigger guards or barrel ends, where a secure grip is critical

You'll also notice knurling on the edge of some coins — those tiny vertical ridges around the rim of a coin serve the same anti-slip function and are a form of knurling.

A knurled surface feels slightly rough and textured — not sharp, not painful, but distinctly not smooth. Running your thumb across it feels like running it over a tiny, rigid grid. It has a satisfying, almost mechanical feel to it, which is partly why knurled surfaces are considered a mark of quality in precision tools and everyday carry items like pens and knives.
The Key Distinction to Keep in Mind

Knurled is not just "rough." A rough surface is random and unintentional — think of sandpaper or a worn surface. A knurled surface is purposefully patterned and regular. Every ridge is placed deliberately. The word carries the strong implication of intentional engineering for a functional purpose (grip), not mere texture for texture's sake.

Knurled = having a precise, repeating pattern of small ridges or diamond-shaped bumps on a surface, put there on purpose to make the object easier to grip and control with your fingers.

If you remember nothing else: knurled means deliberately ridged for grip.
9526:
A koan is a short question, statement, or story used in Zen Buddhism as a tool for meditation. It is specifically designed to be something your logical, rational mind cannot solve — and that's the entire point.

Think of it this way: your everyday mind is like a locked door. Normal thinking, reasoning, and analysis are keys that open most doors in life. A koan is a door that none of those keys fit. You have to find a completely different way through.

The best-known koan in the world is:

"What is the sound of one hand clapping?"

Notice what happens when you read that. Your mind immediately tries to reason it out. Well, clapping requires two hands, so one hand can't make a sound... or maybe it's silence? But every answer your logic produces feels wrong or incomplete. That frustration you feel? That's exactly what a koan is supposed to produce. You're not missing something. The puzzle is built that way on purpose.

Other well-known koans include "What did your face look like before your parents were born?" and "If a tree falls in a forest and no one is there, does it make a sound?" (though the last one is a philosophical question that has been compared to a koan, rather than being one in the traditional sense).
Why Would Anyone Use Something Unsolvable?

In Zen Buddhism, the goal is to reach a state of direct, clear, pure awareness — a sudden flash of deep understanding about the nature of reality and the self. This is called satori (enlightenment or awakening). Zen teachers believe that ordinary logical thinking actually blocks this kind of understanding, because logical thinking is always working with words, concepts, and categories — all of which are just maps of reality, not reality itself.

A koan is a tool to exhaust your logical mind. When you wrestle with a koan long enough and your logical mind finally gives up trying to solve it the "normal" way, something shifts. You stop thinking about the question and instead experience something more direct and intuitive. That shift is what the koan was leading you toward all along.

It's a bit like the difference between reading about the taste of a mango and actually biting into one. No amount of description (logic, words, reasoning) can substitute for the direct experience. A koan is designed to push you past the description and into the experience.
How Koans Are Used in Practice

In traditional Zen training, a student doesn't just read a koan and think about it casually. A Zen master (called a roshi) assigns a specific koan to a specific student based on where that student is in their spiritual development. The student then meditates on it — sometimes for weeks, months, or even years.

Periodically, the student meets privately with the teacher to present their understanding of the koan. This private meeting is called dokusan. The teacher will quickly and firmly reject any answer that comes from intellectual reasoning. Not because the student is stupid, but because the teacher can tell the difference between a clever logical answer and a response that shows genuine, direct understanding.

The "correct" response to a koan is often not a sentence at all. It might be an action, a gesture, a single word, or a silence delivered in a very particular way. What matters is whether it demonstrates that the student has genuinely broken through to a new way of seeing — not that they've constructed a clever argument.
There Are Many Koans, Not Just One

Zen tradition has a large collection of koans, many of them compiled in ancient texts. The most famous collection is called the Blue Cliff Record (from 12th-century China), and another is the Gateless Gate (from 13th-century China). These contain hundreds of koans, each one targeting a different aspect of the student's understanding.

Koans are typically arranged in a kind of curriculum. A beginner might be given a foundational koan like "Mu" (a Japanese word meaning "nothing" or "not," arising from a story about whether a dog has Buddha-nature). More advanced students receive progressively subtler koans. In this way, koans form a complete training system, not just individual puzzles.

It's worth being clear about what a koan is not, because it's easy to confuse it with similar things.

A koan is not a riddle in the ordinary sense. A riddle has a clever logical answer that, once you hear it, makes perfect sense ("I speak without a mouth and hear without ears — I am an echo"). A koan's "resolution" is not like that.

A koan is not a trick question. A trick question misleads you with a false assumption. A koan isn't trying to trick you; it's trying to transform you.

A koan is not unanswerable. This is the most important distinction. It seems unanswerable through logic, but it has a genuine resolution — it's just a resolution that comes from a different mode of understanding, one that Zen practice cultivates.
The Word in Everyday Modern Usage

Today, outside of formal Zen contexts, people sometimes use the word "koan" more loosely in everyday English to describe any question or statement that seems paradoxical, deeply puzzling, or impossible to resolve through ordinary thinking. For example, someone might describe a philosophical dilemma in ethics or science as "almost like a koan."

This looser use is acceptable in casual speech, but it's worth knowing that in its precise, original meaning, a koan is always tied to Zen Buddhist practice — it's a spiritual training tool with a specific tradition, method, and purpose behind it, not just any clever paradox.

A koan is a deliberately paradoxical question or statement from Zen Buddhism, used as a meditation tool to push the mind past logical thinking and toward a moment of direct spiritual insight. It cannot be solved by reasoning. It can only be resolved by a shift in perception — a kind of awakening that no amount of clever thinking can manufacture, but that deep, sustained meditation on the koan is meant to bring about.

If you ever feel genuinely baffled by a koan, you're engaging with it correctly. The bafflement is the beginning of the practice.
9527: A kobold is a type of supernatural creature — a spirit or goblin-like being — that comes from old German and broader European folklore. Think of it as a small, magical entity that exists somewhere between a helpful household servant and a troublesome, mischievous imp. Whether it helps you or harms you depends almost entirely on how you treat it.

Kobolds in folklore appear in two main settings, each with a slightly different character.

1. The Household Kobold

This is the most classic form. A household kobold is an invisible (or rarely-seen) spirit that attaches itself to a specific home or family. It takes up residence there — often in a barn, cellar, hearth, or stable — and considers that place its own.

When treated well, a household kobold is remarkably useful. It might:

  • Do chores quietly while the family sleeps
  • Care for the animals
  • Protect the home from misfortune
  • Warn the family of danger

The "payment" it expects is small but non-negotiable: a bowl of porridge or a little food left out for it regularly. It craves respect and acknowledgment.

When ignored, disrespected, or mistreated, it turns nasty — and fast. It might:

  • Sour the milk
  • Tangle people's hair while they sleep
  • Hide objects
  • Make livestock sick
  • Generally cause chaos in the home

The household kobold does not forgive easily. It has a long memory and a short temper when its pride is wounded.

2. The Mine Kobold

This type lives underground, deep in mines and caves. Mine kobolds were feared by miners across medieval Germany and Central Europe. They were blamed for cave-ins, equipment failures, strange noises underground (like knocking or tapping sounds in the rock), and the disappearance of miners. They were seen as guardians of the earth's hidden resources — resources they did not want humans to take.

Interestingly, the chemical element cobalt gets its name from kobolds. Medieval miners kept finding a certain ore that looked like it should contain silver but didn't, and smelting it released toxic fumes. Frustrated and frightened, they blamed kobolds for the deception — they believed the spirits had replaced the silver with this useless, poisonous rock as a trick.

Here is where things get interesting: kobolds don't have one fixed appearance. In folklore, they're shape-shifting or simply invisible most of the time. When they do take a visible form, they often look like:

  • A small, old man in raggedy or simple peasant clothing
  • A child-sized humanoid figure
  • Occasionally an animal, a flame, or even a piece of wood

They are consistently described as small — never tall or imposing. Their power comes from their magic and their connection to a place, not from physical strength.

Today, the word "kobold" is most commonly encountered in fantasy fiction, tabletop games (like Dungeons & Dragons), and video games. In these modern contexts, the kobold has been reimagined significantly and looks quite different from its folklore roots.

In modern fantasy, kobolds are typically:

  • Small, reptilian humanoids — scaly, somewhat lizard-like or dragon-like in appearance
  • Portrayed as weak individually but dangerous in large groups
  • Often described as clever trap-makers and tunnelers
  • Depicted as either cowardly (running from a fight) or cunning (setting up ambushes)
  • Frequently cast as minor enemies or low-level antagonists that adventurers encounter early in a story

This modern kobold is essentially its own creature — it shares the name and the underground, trickster-ish personality with the folklore version, but visually and conceptually it has evolved into something quite distinct.

The word "kobold" is always a noun. You use it to refer to one of these creatures directly:

  • "The farmer left porridge by the hearth for the kobold every night."
  • "According to legend, a kobold had haunted the mine for centuries."
  • "The adventurers were ambushed by a pack of kobolds in the tunnel."

The plural is simply kobolds.

A kobold represents a very old human idea: that invisible, powerful beings share our spaces with us — our homes, our mines, our earth — and that our relationship with them is fragile. Treat them with respect, and they help. Ignore or insult them, and they make your life miserable. The kobold is a small creature, but in the world of folklore, it punches well above its weight.
9528: Kohl is a dark substance — almost always black or very dark grey — that people apply around their eyes as a cosmetic. Think of it as the ancient world's eye makeup: part eyeliner, part eye shadow, all in one.

Traditional kohl is an extremely fine, soft powder or paste made from natural minerals ground down until they're almost silky smooth. The most common ingredient historically was galena, a naturally occurring mineral that is essentially a dark, metallic grey-black material. Other versions were made from antimony sulfide (another dark mineral), charcoal, soot from oil lamps, or burnt almonds — sometimes blended with oils or fats to make a paste.

It is stored in a small container called a kohl pot or kohl jar, which is often beautifully decorated. To apply it, you dip a thin stick (made from wood, ivory, bone, or metal) into the pot and carefully draw it along the inner rim of the eyelid, along the upper lash line, or beneath the eye. The result is a bold, dark, slightly smoky outline that makes the eyes look dramatically defined.
Where it comes from and who uses it

Kohl is not a niche or exotic product — it has one of the longest and most widespread histories of any cosmetic in human existence.

Ancient Egypt is probably the most famous example. In paintings and carvings of ancient Egyptians, you always notice that thick, dramatic dark line around their eyes. That is kohl — and importantly, both men and women wore it. Pharaohs, priests, commoners — everyone used it.

Beyond Egypt, kohl has been central to beauty culture across the Middle East, North Africa, and South Asia for thousands of years. In the Arab world, it is known as kuhl (the word "kohl" in English actually comes from Arabic). In India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh, a near-identical substance is called kajal or surma, and it is deeply woven into everyday life — not just as beauty product, but as part of cultural rituals, including putting it on newborn babies' eyes.

The reasons are layered and fascinating:

For beauty: The most obvious reason. Kohl makes eyes look larger, more intense, more expressive, and more striking. The smoky dark outline creates a powerful visual contrast, especially on lighter-coloured eyes, but equally dramatic on dark eyes.

For sun protection: In the scorching, sun-drenched climates of North Africa and the Middle East, the dark pigment applied around the eyes served a practical purpose — reducing the glare from the sun, much like how modern athletes put black grease beneath their eyes before games.

For perceived medicinal protection: People historically believed kohl could shield eyes from infections, dust, and disease. Interestingly, some researchers have suggested that certain ancient formulations may have had mild antibacterial properties, though this is still debated.

For spiritual and cultural protection: In many cultures, kohl is believed to ward off the "evil eye" — the idea that an envious or malicious gaze from another person can cause harm. Applying kohl, especially on children, was seen as a form of spiritual shielding.

Today, you will encounter the word "kohl" in two contexts:

1. Traditional kohl — still used in parts of the Middle East, South Asia, and North Africa in its original mineral-powder form. Health authorities now caution against lead-based versions (more on that below), but non-lead alternatives made from antimony or plant-based ingredients are still widely used.

2. Modern cosmetic products labelled "kohl" — Walk into any beauty shop and you'll see "kohl pencil" or "kohl eyeliner" on the shelves. These products are designed to replicate the dark, smoky, smudged look of traditional kohl, but they are made from modern synthetic and safer ingredients. They are not the same material as traditional kohl — they just borrow the name and the aesthetic.

Traditional kohl made from lead-based minerals is now known to be dangerous. Lead is a toxic substance that can be absorbed through the sensitive skin around the eyes, and it poses a serious health risk — especially to children. Many countries now ban or strictly regulate the import and sale of traditional lead-based kohl. If you ever see traditional kohl being sold, it's worth checking what it's made from. Modern products labelled "kohl" in mainstream shops are safe because they use regulated cosmetic ingredients.

Kohl is a finely powdered or pasted dark mineral cosmetic, applied around the eyes using a stick. It has been used for thousands of years across ancient Egypt, the Arab world, and South Asia — by men and women alike — for beauty, sun protection, and cultural or spiritual reasons. Today, the word also refers broadly to a style of dark, smoky eye cosmetic in mainstream beauty products. It sits at a rare intersection of art, culture, history, and daily life — a word that carries the weight of entire civilisations in it.
9529: A kohlrabi is a vegetable. More specifically, it is a plant whose swollen, round stem is the main edible part. It belongs to the same plant family as cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kale, and Brussels sprouts — a family known for being nutritious and widely eaten around the world.

Most vegetables you eat underground are roots (like carrots) or tubers (like potatoes). Kohlrabi is different — its round, ball-like edible part grows above the ground, sitting right at soil level. This rounded, swollen part is actually a thickened stem, not a root. This makes it a fairly unique-looking vegetable.

Thin stalks with flat leaves grow outward directly from this round stem, giving the whole plant a slightly alien, almost spacecraft-like appearance — like a round ball with antennae sticking out of it.

• Shape: Round, roughly the size of a tennis ball, though it can grow as large as a grapefruit if left in the ground longer.
  • Outer skin color: Either pale green or deep purple, depending on the variety. Both varieties are the same on the inside.
  • Inner flesh: Always pale white or creamy white, regardless of the outer color.
  • Texture: Firm and crisp, much like the thick stem of a broccoli head.
  • Leaves: Green, flat, and edible, sprouting from the sides of the round stem on thin stalks.

Kohlrabi has a mild, slightly sweet flavor. The closest comparison is the taste of a broccoli stem — but milder, a little juicier, and with a very faint hint of pepper. Some people also compare it to a mild turnip or a sweet, delicate cabbage. It is not bitter, not sharp, and not overpowering — it is a gentle, pleasant-tasting vegetable.

When eaten raw, it is crunchy and refreshing. When cooked, it becomes soft and tender, and its sweetness comes out a little more.

Both main parts of the kohlrabi plant are edible:

  1. The round stem (the bulb): This is the primary edible part. The tough outer skin is peeled away first, and the pale flesh inside is what is eaten — raw or cooked.
  2. The leaves: These are also edible and can be cooked in the same way you would cook kale or spinach — sautéed, added to soups, or steamed.
How Is It Used in Cooking?

Kohlrabi is a very flexible vegetable in the kitchen. Here are the common ways it appears:

  • Raw: Peeled and sliced thinly or cut into sticks, it can be eaten as a snack, added to salads, or used in coleslaw for a crunchy texture.
  • Cooked: It can be roasted, steamed, boiled, stir-fried, or added to soups and curries. Heat softens it and brings out a pleasant, natural sweetness.
  • Stuffed: Large kohlrabi bulbs are sometimes hollowed out and stuffed with a filling, then baked — a popular preparation in some European cuisines.
  • Grated: It can be grated and used in fritters or mixed into dishes where a mild, crunchy element is needed.

It is especially common in German, Eastern European, Indian (particularly Kashmiri), and Vietnamese cuisines.
How Does It Fit Into the Vegetable World?

Kohlrabi is classified as a stem vegetable — because the part you mainly eat is a swollen stem. This puts it in an interesting category alongside things like celery (which is also a stem). It is not a root vegetable, not a leafy green, and not a fruit-vegetable like a tomato. It sits in its own neat corner as a swollen, above-ground stem that happens to be delicious.

Kohlrabi is a round, above-ground, stem vegetable with pale green or purple skin and crisp white flesh, mild and slightly sweet in taste, belonging to the cabbage family, and eaten both raw and cooked.
9530: A kookaburra is a type of bird native to Australia and New Guinea. It is the largest member of the kingfisher family — a group of birds traditionally known for fishing — though the kookaburra is famous for being a kingfisher that doesn't really need to fish. Instead of hunting near water like most of its relatives, it thrives in forests, woodlands, and even the backyards of Australian suburbs.

The kookaburra is a chunky, stocky bird — roughly the size of a large pigeon, measuring around 28 to 45 centimetres (11 to 17 inches) from beak to tail. Its most striking feature is its oversized head and long, powerful beak, which give it a bold, almost comical look.

Its feathers are mainly brown and creamy white. The most well-known species — the Laughing Kookaburra — has a distinctive dark brown stripe running across each eye, like a robber's mask. Some species also show patches of blue on their wings, making them remarkably beautiful up close.

This is the kookaburra's most defining characteristic, and the reason most people know the word. The kookaburra produces a call that sounds almost exactly like loud, rollicking human laughter — a rising "hoo hoo hoo ha ha ha HA HA HA!" that echoes across the bush.

This laugh is so iconic that Hollywood has used it for decades in movies and TV shows to suggest a jungle or wild setting — even scenes set in Africa or South America — despite it being a purely Australian sound. The call is used by kookaburras to mark their territory, warning other birds to stay away. Families of kookaburras often laugh together, creating a chorus that can be heard from a great distance. They are especially vocal at dawn and dusk, which is why Australians have long thought of the kookaburra's laugh as a natural alarm clock and sundown bell.

Despite its relation to the fish-eating kingfishers, the kookaburra is a dedicated meat-eater of the land. It hunts and eats:

  • Insects and worms
  • Lizards and small reptiles
  • Mice and other small rodents
  • Small birds
  • Snakes — including venomous ones

Yes, the kookaburra is famous for being a snake hunter. It will swoop down from a branch, grab a snake in its powerful beak, and then beat it against a hard surface (like a rock or tree branch) repeatedly until the snake is dead or stunned — only then does it swallow its meal. This behaviour protects the bird from being bitten and is a remarkable feat of instinct and precision.

The kookaburra hunts mostly by sitting still and watching patiently from a perch, then diving down swiftly the moment it spots prey below. Think of it as an aerial sniper with excellent eyesight.

The kookaburra is found primarily in eastern and southeastern Australia, in habitats ranging from dense eucalyptus (gum tree) forests to open woodlands. It has also been introduced to Western Australia, Tasmania, and New Zealand. Over time, it has adapted very well to suburban and urban environments, comfortably living near humans and occasionally stealing food right off barbecue plates — a habit that has made it both beloved and mischievous in Australian culture.

Kookaburras are social, family-oriented birds. They live in small groups made up of a breeding pair and their older offspring from previous years. These older "helper" birds assist in raising younger siblings — feeding them, protecting the nest, and teaching them to call. This kind of cooperative family structure is relatively rare in the bird world and makes the kookaburra stand out as an unusually loyal and community-minded creature.

They are also highly territorial, and that famous laugh is their primary tool for defending their patch of land. Once a kookaburra family claims a territory, they defend it fiercely with their voices.

There are four species of kookaburra:

1. The Laughing Kookaburra — The most famous and widespread. This is the one with the iconic laugh and the "masked" face. It's the largest of the four and the one most people picture when they hear the word.

2. The Blue-winged Kookaburra — Found in northern Australia and southern New Guinea. It has striking blue patches on its wings and tail and a slightly harsher, more chaotic-sounding call compared to the laughing kookaburra.

3. The Spangled Kookaburra — Found in New Guinea and nearby islands. It is smaller and has beautifully speckled (spangled) blue and white feathers.

4. The Rufous-bellied Kookaburra — Also found in New Guinea. It has a warm, reddish-orange belly and is the smallest and most elusive of the four.

When people say "kookaburra" without any further detail, they almost always mean the Laughing Kookaburra.

In Australia, the kookaburra holds a place of deep cultural affection. It appears in one of the country's most well-known children's songs: "Kookaburra sits in the old gum tree, merry merry king of the bush is he…" — a song taught to generations of Australian schoolchildren. The bird is a symbol of the Australian bush experience, representing wild, carefree, sun-drenched nature.

It has also been used as a mascot for major Australian sporting events and is one of the most recognisable symbols of the country's unique wildlife — right alongside kangaroos and koalas.

A kookaburra is a large, stocky, carnivorous kingfisher bird from Australia, best known for its extraordinary call that sounds like human laughter, its fearless ability to hunt and kill snakes, its devoted family social life, and its place as one of the most beloved symbols of the Australian natural world. It is a bird that is impossible to mistake once you've heard it laugh.
9531:
Kooky means slightly crazy, strange, or eccentric in a harmless and often charming way. When you call something or someone kooky, you are saying they are a little odd, unusual, or unpredictable — but not in a scary or seriously worrying way. There is almost always a hint of warmth or amusement in the word.

Think of it this way: if "crazy" is a storm, kooky is a light drizzle. It describes the gentle, quirky, lovably weird end of the spectrum.

This is what makes kooky special — it is not a harsh or insulting word. It carries a playful, affectionate, or amused tone. When someone calls a person kooky, they usually mean it with a smile, not a frown. It suggests that the strangeness is:

  • Harmless — nobody is getting hurt by it
  • Entertaining — it makes life a little more interesting
  • Genuine — the person is just being themselves, not trying to be normal

If someone says "She's a little kooky," they probably find her charming and amusing, not dangerous or disturbing.

However, context matters. The same word can occasionally carry a mild, gentle criticism — like saying someone is a bit too out there or not entirely sensible. But even then, it is never strongly negative. It never implies evil, violence, or serious mental illness. It stays in the soft, light-hearted zone.
What Can Be Described as Kooky?

The word can describe people, behavior, ideas, things, or places. Here are examples of each:

A person:

"My neighbor is kooky — she talks to her plants, names her houseplants after historical figures, and wears a different hat every single day."

The neighbor is not dangerous. She is just charmingly odd.

Behavior or habits:

"He has a kooky habit of organizing his bookshelf by the color of the covers instead of the author's name."

Unusual? Yes. Harmful? Not at all.

An idea or plan:

"It sounds like a kooky idea, but what if we painted the entire office ceiling sky blue with clouds?"

It's an unconventional idea that makes you raise an eyebrow and maybe smile.

A thing or place:

"They stayed at a kooky little hotel shaped like a giant shoe."

Strange, whimsical, and memorable — in a fun way.

Kooky sits at a mild-to-moderate level of strangeness. If you imagine a scale from perfectly normal to completely out of touch with reality, kooky sits somewhere in the lower-middle — noticeably odd, but nowhere near alarming.

  • A person who always hums while eating → slightly kooky
  • A person who believes the moon is made of cheese and makes life decisions based on this belief → very kooky
