The word "landlord" applies in all these cases. In everyday conversation, though, when people say "landlord," they usually mean someone who rents out a home or apartment.

The landlord and tenant enter into a formal agreement called a lease or a rental agreement. This is usually a written contract that spells out:

  • How much rent the tenant must pay, and how often (usually monthly).
  • How long the tenant can stay (e.g., one year, or month-to-month).
  • Rules about the property (no pets, no loud noise at night, etc.).
  • What happens if either side breaks the agreement.

Once this agreement is signed, the tenant has the legal right to occupy that property for the agreed period — even though the landlord still owns it. This is a crucial point: ownership and occupancy are two separate things. The landlord owns it, but the tenant has the right to live there and use it as their home.
What the Landlord Is Responsible For

Being a landlord is not just about collecting rent. A landlord typically has several duties:

  • Maintaining the property — keeping it safe, functional, and liveable. If the roof leaks or the plumbing breaks, it is generally the landlord's responsibility to fix it (unless the tenant caused the damage).
  • Not disturbing the tenant — the landlord cannot simply walk into the property whenever they want. In most places, law requires the landlord to give the tenant advance notice before entering.
  • Returning the security deposit — at the start of a tenancy, landlords often collect a security deposit (an extra sum of money held as protection in case of damage). At the end, if the tenant has cared for the property properly, the landlord must return this deposit.
What the Landlord Has the Right to Do

In return, the landlord has rights too:

  • To receive rent on time. If the tenant stops paying, the landlord can take legal steps to remove them — a process called eviction.
  • To set reasonable rules for the property, within the limits of the law.
  • To not renew the lease when it expires, meaning the landlord can decide not to continue renting to that tenant after the agreed period ends.
  • To sell the property — though the tenant's rights during their lease period are usually protected even if the property is sold.

Imagine Priya owns a two-bedroom flat in Mumbai but lives in Bangalore for work. She doesn't need the flat herself right now, so she rents it out. She advertises it, finds a family who wants to live there, signs a one-year lease with them, and they pay her ₹25,000 every month. Priya is the landlord. The family are her tenants. The ₹25,000 is the rent.

If the ceiling fan stops working, it's Priya's job to get it fixed. If the family leaves muddy footprints on the walls and damages the paint, she can deduct that cost from their security deposit. If they stop paying rent for three months, she has legal grounds to begin the eviction process.

For many landlords, renting out property is a source of income — sometimes their main income, sometimes just extra income alongside a regular job. Owning property and renting it to others is a well-known way to build wealth, because:

  1. The rent income comes in steadily every month.
  2. The property itself may increase in value over time.

Some people own just one rental flat; others own dozens of apartments or even entire buildings. When someone owns a very large number of properties and rents them all out, they are sometimes called a property investor or, in a more formal context, a real estate investor — though "landlord" still applies to them.

In informal speech, the word can sometimes be used loosely to refer to the owner of a pub or inn who also runs the place (an old-fashioned usage, especially in British English). But in modern, everyday usage — in India, the US, the UK, and most of the world — "landlord" almost always means: someone who owns property and rents it out to a tenant.

A landlord owns a property → rents it to a tenant → tenant pays rent → landlord is responsible for maintaining the property → both sides have rights and duties under a lease agreement.

That is the complete picture of what a landlord is.

A landlubber is a person who has little or no experience with the sea, ships, or sailing. In short, it's someone who has spent their life on land and is therefore unfamiliar with — and usually clumsy or uncomfortable in — the world of ships and seafaring.

The word belongs to the vocabulary of sailors. When an experienced sailor calls someone a landlubber, they mean: this person does not know ships, does not know the sea, and it shows.
The full picture of its meaning

The word does not just mean "a person who lives on land." Virtually everyone lives on land — that alone doesn't make you a landlubber. The key element is inexperience and unfamiliarity with the sea. A landlubber is someone who:

  • Has never (or rarely) been on a ship or boat
  • Does not understand how ships work, how to navigate, or how to handle the sea
  • Gets seasick, stumbles on a rocking deck, or generally seems lost and helpless aboard a vessel
  • Has no grasp of nautical skills, terms, or traditions

Think of it like this: if you dropped a landlubber onto a sailing ship, they would be confused, awkward, and out of their depth — while an experienced sailor would feel completely at home.
The tone: slightly mocking, but not always harsh

The word carries a mildly contemptuous or teasing tone when used by sailors. It implies that the person being called a landlubber is naive, unskilled, or simply not built for life at sea. There's a subtle "us vs. them" attitude embedded in the word — we are the sailors, they are the landlubbers.

However, the mockery is rarely vicious. The word can be used:

  • Teasingly, in a light and playful way ("Come on, you landlubber, stop holding the railing!")
  • Affectionately, among friends who know someone is not a sea person
  • Self-deprecatingly, when someone admits their own cluelessness about the sea ("I'm just a landlubber — I've never even been on a canoe")
  • Contemptuously, by a gruff sailor genuinely dismissing someone's lack of seafaring ability

So depending on the situation and the speaker's tone, the word can range from gentle teasing to outright dismissal.
Who uses this word, and about whom

Landlubber is a word used by people with sea experience to describe people without it. Sailors, pirates, fishermen, naval officers — anyone who considers themselves a person of the sea might use this word for someone they see as firmly rooted to the land.

Historically, the word was common in maritime culture, where the distinction between sailors and non-sailors was a very real and serious divide. Life at sea required completely different skills, knowledge, and toughness compared to life on land.

In everyday modern life, landlubber is not a common word. You won't hear it in normal conversations very often. It belongs more to:

  • Historical fiction and literature set at sea or in naval/pirate eras
  • Pirate-themed movies, TV shows, and games (it's a classic "pirate word")
  • Nautical and sailing communities, where it may still be used genuinely or humorously
  • Casual, playful speech, when someone wants to tease a friend about being inexperienced on the water

Despite being old-fashioned, the word is still widely understood. If you called someone a landlubber today, most people would immediately understand what you meant — even if they'd never used the word themselves. It has a theatrical, slightly old-world feel to it, which is part of why it survives in pirate stories and sea adventures.

• "You call yourself a sailor? You're nothing but a landlubber!" — a veteran sailor dismissing a newcomer.
  • "As a complete landlubber, she gripped the railing and turned pale the moment the ship began to rock."
  • "The pirates sneered at the landlubbers who had clearly never spent a day at sea in their lives."
  • "Don't worry — even the greatest sailors were landlubbers once."
  • "I'll admit it: I'm a landlubber through and through. The thought of a two-week ocean voyage makes me nervous."

A landlubber is someone with no experience of the sea or ships — someone who belongs to the land, not the water. The word is used by sailors (and in nautical or pirate contexts) to describe such a person, usually with a hint of mockery or condescension, though it can also be used lightly or affectionately. It's informal, a little old-fashioned, and today is most alive in historical stories, pirate lore, and playful conversation.
